name: Crown lengthening / gingivectomy

lead: Crown lengthening and gingivectomy reshape the gum line so more of each tooth shows and less gum appears when you smile. They suit gummy smiles where the gum line itself is the cause.

Gum tissue is removed in gingivectomy, and crown lengthening can also recontour the supporting bone, so the gum line sits higher on the teeth. These are standard periodontal procedures, and registered trials compare surgical, flapless, piezoelectric, laser and digitally guided methods.

paras: A dentist or periodontist does it in the chair, trimming or repositioning gum with bone recontouring if needed. The change in tooth display is visible once the area has healed. People often use it as one step in a wider smile plan.
Described drawbacks include irreversible bone loss, weakening of neighbouring teeth, pain with flap surgery, recurrence and black triangles between teeth. Bone removal cannot be undone.

angle.text: Crown lengthening and gingivectomy reshape the gum line so teeth look longer and less gum shows, used for gummy smiles where the gum line is the cause. Gum and sometimes bone are trimmed back, and the change in tooth display is visible once healed.

lead: Crown lengthening exposes more tooth by removing gum tissue and sometimes supporting bone, and is done for functional or aesthetic reasons, including gummy smile.[1] Gingivectomy is the removal of part of the gum tissue and is described as the oldest surgical approach in periodontal therapy.[2]

Both are established dental procedures used for restorative and periodontal reasons; their use for smile aesthetics is the part relevant to looksmaxxing. Registered trials in 2011-2026 compare techniques such as flapless, piezoelectric, laser and digitally guided approaches.[3][4][5]
infobox: Gingivectomy, flap with bone recontouring, forced eruption, laser

paras: Crown lengthening may be done surgically by an apically repositioned flap with bone recontouring, or orthodontically by forced tooth eruption.[1] Gingivectomy can be performed with a scalpel, electrosurgery or laser.[2]

Wikipedia states that up to about 3 mm of gum display when smiling is considered acceptable and more is often regarded as unaesthetic, and that gingivectomy can address it.[2] Aesthetic planning must consider smile line, lip position and tooth proportions.[2] Trials treat conditions such as altered passive eruption.[6][7]

Described drawbacks include encroaching on the supracrestal tissue attachment, weakening adjacent teeth by removing bone, bone loss that is hard to restore, and postoperative pain with the flap technique.[1] For gingivectomy, recurrence, black triangles and return of disease with poor hygiene are described.[2]

Registered trials include a comparison of periodontal plastic surgery techniques for gummy smile (n=30),[8] digitally guided versus conventional crown lengthening,[9][10] flapless esthetic crown lengthening for excessive gingival display (n=28, 2011),[3] closed piezoelectric versus open flap approaches,[11][6] Er:YAG laser versus surgical crown lengthening,[4] and periodontal stability after correcting altered passive eruption.[7] Published results are not summarised in the sources used.
